heroText: Copenhagen is Denmark's harbour capital, known for bikes, design, food and easy water-level sightseeing. Start at Nyhavn, spend an evening in Tivoli Gardens, then link Christiansborg Palace, Rosenborg Castle and the harbour baths by metro or bike. Copenhagen Airport is directly connected by metro and rail, making arrivals fast.

areas.name: Indre By
areas.text: Indre By is the historic centre, best for first visits near Nyhavn, shopping streets and major royal sights.

areas.name: Vesterbro
areas.text: Vesterbro has restaurants, nightlife, the central station and meatpacking-district energy close to Tivoli.

areas.name: Nørrebro
areas.text: Nørrebro is diverse and lively, with casual food, bars, parks and better value than the old centre.

areas.name: Christianshavn
areas.text: Christianshavn offers canals, harbour walks and easy access to Christiania and the opera side of the city.

airports.name: Copenhagen Airport (CPH)
airports.text: Copenhagen Airport sits on Amager and has direct metro and rail links to the city centre and Sweden.

airportTransfer.value: 13-20 min by metro or train to central Copenhagen
airportTransfer.distance: about 8 km southeast of the centre

stayOverview: Indre By is the classic first base, Vesterbro suits food and nightlife near the station, Nørrebro gives a more local and better-value stay, and Christianshavn is ideal for canals and harbour walks.
hotelIntro: Copenhagen is easy by metro, bike and harbour routes. Central hotels are convenient but pricey, while Vesterbro, Nørrebro and Christianshavn often give stronger neighbourhood character and better evenings.
rentalCars: Do not rent for Copenhagen; bikes, metro, trains and walking are much easier than parking.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Choose Indre By for a first short stay, or Vesterbro if food, nightlife and station access matter more.

travelTips.title: Airport metro
travelTips.text: The airport metro runs directly into central areas, so taxis are rarely necessary unless carrying heavy luggage.

travelTips.title: Cycling
travelTips.text: Rent a bike only if you are confident in busy cycle lanes; otherwise use metro and harbour buses.

travelTips.title: Day trip
travelTips.text: Keep one side-trip day flexible from Copenhagen, then choose it only after checking transport frequency and opening hours.

history.label: 12th century
history.text: The earliest written mention of the town was in the 12th century when Saxo Grammaticus in Gesta Danorum referred to it as Portus Mercatorum, meaning "Merchants' Harbour" or, in the Danish of the time.
Traditionally, Copenhagen's founding has been dated to Bishop Absalon's construction of a modest fortress on the little island of Slotsholmen in 1167 where Christiansborg Palace stands today.
Defensive ramparts and moats were completed, and by 1177 St.
In 1254, it received a city charter under Bishop Jakob Erlandsen who garnered support from the local fishing merchants against the king by granting them special privileges.

With the establishment of the Kalmar Union (1397–1523) between Denmark, Norway and Sweden, by about 1416 Copenhagen had emerged as the capital of Denmark when Eric of Pomerania moved his seat to Copenhagen Castle.
The University of Copenhagen was inaugurated on 1 June 1479 by King Christian I, following approval from Pope Sixtus IV.
It was successfully besieged in 1523 by the forces of Frederik I, who supported Lutheranism.

In 1733, work began on the royal residence of Christiansborg Palace, completed in 1745.

An important development for the city was the opening of the Copenhagen Metro railway system in 2002.

history.text: Attacks by the Wends continued, and after the original fortress was eventually destroyed by the marauders, islanders replaced it with Copenhagen Castle.
